summary: For ages 9–11, build the idea that gravity is a non-contact attractive force the Earth exerts on anything with mass, pulling objects toward the Earth's centre ('down'). Gravity acts on all objects with mass — light ones as well as heavy ones, and objects in water too — not only on heavy things; the force is actually larger on heavier objects, but that does not make them fall faster. The core teaching battle is the intuitive Aristotelian belief that heavier objects fall faster; in negligible air resistance all objects fall at the same rate, while in air, air resistance (not weaker gravity) slows light, non-compact objects. Equally important is guarding against the over-correction 'everything always falls together,' which is only true when air resistance is negligible. Use predict-observe-explain drops, an air-versus-vacuum comparison, everyday examples of gravity in action (dropping, jumping, water flowing downhill), and the Apollo 15 Moon hammer-and-feather case, plus an orbit-as-continual-falling reframe for 'no gravity in space.'
misconceptions: Heavier objects fall faster (Aristotelian; appears from age 5; Potvin et al.)
Over-correction: all objects always fall at the same rate (only true in a vacuum / when air resistance is negligible; teachers are strong adherents)
There is no gravity in space or on the Moon; gravity needs air/an atmosphere to act
Gravity is magnetism / the Earth is a giant magnet
Gravity acts only on heavy objects, or does not act on objects in water
Astronauts float because there is 'no gravity' — actually they are in continual free-fall (orbit)

activities.title: Air vs vacuum: strip the air and watch mass stop affecting how fast things fall
steps: First predict which lands first when a hammer and a feather are dropped side by side (from rest) in a tall chamber full of air, and write down WHY.
Drop them in air and observe: the feather drifts down slowly, the hammer lands first.
Remove the air from the chamber (e.g. a pump control or vacuum toggle) and drop again; observe the feather and hammer fall together and strike the bottom at the same instant.
Use mass sliders to set extreme heavy/light pairs and check the same-rate result still holds in vacuum.
State in your own words what was actually holding the feather back in air, and whether an object's mass changes how fast it falls once the air is removed.
activities.insight: In negligible air resistance, objects of different mass fall at the same rate; the slower fall of a feather in air is caused by air resistance, not by weaker gravity. Gravity still pulls harder on heavier objects, but the fall rate does not depend on mass once air is removed.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain drops with real objects
steps: Hold a large stone and a small stone at the same height; predict which lands first and say WHY before dropping.
Drop them together and observe that they land at about the same time.
For contrast, drop a flat sheet of paper against a crumpled ball of the SAME paper and observe the difference.
Explain what the two observations together show about gravity's pull versus air resistance, writing the pre-drop reason next to what actually happened.
activities.insight: Gravity pulls on both stones and they fall at nearly the same rate, because air resistance has only a small effect on compact stones over a short drop; changing only the shape of the same paper changes the fall because of air resistance, separating the effect of air resistance from weight.

activities.title: The Moon case: gravity without air
steps: Examine a labelled Moon scene (hammer, feather, weight arrow pointing toward the surface) and the Apollo 15 drop where a hammer and feather were released together.
Predict and then observe what happens when the hammer and feather are dropped on the airless Moon.
Explain what the result shows about whether gravity exists on the Moon and in space, and why the feather no longer flutters.
Tap labelled parts of the scene to reveal facts (e.g. no air, weaker gravity than Earth, objects still fall).
activities.insight: Objects fall on the Moon and fall together because there is gravity (just weaker than Earth's) and no air; 'no gravity in space/on the Moon' is incorrect.

activities.title: Ask an astronaut: why do astronauts float?
steps: Pose questions to an in-role astronaut persona about why astronauts appear to float in orbit.
Articulate, in your own words, that astronauts float because they are in continual free-fall (orbit), not because gravity is absent.
Distinguish 'no gravity' from 'continually falling around the Earth' and explain which is correct.
activities.insight: Weightlessness in orbit is continual free-fall, not the absence of gravity; gravity still acts on astronauts.

activities.title: Retrieval, prediction, and everyday examples
steps: Answer predict-which-lands-first questions for pairs of objects under stated conditions (in air vs in a vacuum).
Sequence or match conditions (air vs vacuum, flat vs crumpled, Earth vs Moon) to outcomes.
Answer a short question on whether there is gravity in space / on the Moon and justify the choice.
Decide whether gravity acts on a very light object (e.g. a leaf) and on an object held underwater, and justify why — gravity still pulls on both because they have mass.
Give everyday examples of gravity in action (dropping objects, jumping and coming back down, water flowing downhill) and explain what gravity is doing in each.
activities.insight: Consolidates the rule 'same rate when air resistance is negligible, otherwise air resistance slows light non-compact objects', that gravity acts in space and on the Moon, and that gravity acts on ALL objects with mass — light ones and objects in water included, not only heavy things.

checkQuestion: I hold a big heavy stone in one hand and a small light stone in the other, at the same height, and let go of both at the exact same moment. Which one hits the ground first — and why do you think that?
checkAnswer: They hit the ground at about the same time. Earth's gravity pulls down on every object; it pulls harder on the heavier stone, but the heavier stone is also harder to speed up, so both gain speed at the same rate and land together. Only something very light and flat, like a feather, falls more slowly — because of air resistance, not weaker gravity.
